newsitem.title: USA: New Products on horizon to remove hair.
newsitem.headline: New Products on horizon to remove hair.

text.p: Gone are the days of "shave and a haircut -- two bits." Today, American men and women spend billions of dollars every year removing unwanted body hair. According to a new survey, many are willing to spend even more, something that will likely lead the personal care industry to develop new alternatives to shaving.
The majority of Americans are willing to spend money to remove unwanted hair, said the survey by The BrainWaves Group, for ThermoLase Corp., maker of SoftLight, a laser-based hair removal technique.

Hair is as much as style factor as hemlines and tie width. No longer is the hirsute male a la Tom Selleck the ideal as he was in the 1980s. According to the survey of 505 adults aged 18 and over, conducted by telephone in March, 67 percent of women said hairy men "turn them off."
Among men, hirsute women are a "turn off" to 84 percent.
"The subject of hair is a highly emotional one," said John Hansen, president of ThermoLase, based in San Diego.

"For Americans in particular, their hair makes a statement about their sexuality, self-esteem and pride -- and how others view excess hair is tied to their overall feling of attractiveness and self-respect."
Men, however, said that body hair makes them feel more masculine (60 percent). Only 12 percent of men expressed interest in the removal of unwanted body hair.

About 21 percent of those surveyed spend $10 or more per month on the removal of unwanted hair, especially shaving. On average, about 48 percent of men and women surveyed said they spend under $5 a month on the removal of unwanted hair from their faces or elsewhere.

However, 40 percent of people who spend a least $1 a month on the removal of unwanted hair, and are extremely interested in new methods of hair removal, are willing to spend $100 or more per year to remove unwanted hair.
Nearly one quarter said they are extremely/very interested in trying a new hair removal system and 51 percent said they are at least somewhat interested.
What might some of these new methods be? One is the use of laser, such as ThermoLase's product, but currently lasers are used by far less than 1 percent of the population.
Elvis Presley lives on in song, and now, in food. The first live-entertainment restaurant to bear the entertainer's name will open July 25 in Memphis, Tenn., home to Presley's mansion, Graceland.

Elvis Presley's Memphis, located at 126 Beale St., corner of 2nd and Beale, is a 330-seat, full-service restaurant with three bars and five dining rooms, all with a full view of The Memphis Showroom, the main stage.
In addition to a retail shop, the billiard table on which Elvis played with The Beatles will be housed in the The Bel Air Billiard Room.
Elvis' wife, Priscilla, and his daughter, Lisa Marie, will host the opening night party.
For more information, call 901-527-6900.

A new music video for tots, "Sing it Again," has made its debut. This sing-along video is designed for children ages 3 months to 5 years and features such classics as "Itsy, Bitsy Spider" and "The Bus Song."
It features music therapist and early childhood music instructor Nicole Allgood.
The video by Golden Hour Productions of Chicago is 30 minutes long. It sells for $14.95.
For more information, call 800-735-8468.
